original_question: Determine the maximum number of circles of radius 1 that can be placed inside a circle of radius n so that no two overlap except possibly by tangency. More generally, study the analogous problem for variable radii i(n), for packing unit circles into a given triangle, and for analogous packing problems involving spheres, cones, cylinders, regular pyramids, and other planar or spatial figures.
target_in_paper: Unsolved Problem 8, on pages 9-10 of the paper: the maximum-number-of-circles packing question together with its immediately stated Bencze generalization and the closely adjoining triangle / higher-dimensional analogues. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies the main problem of maximizing the number of unit circles inside a circle of radius n under a tangency-allowed, non-overlap condition, and it also preserves the paper's immediately appended extensions: circles of radius i(n) in a circle of radius n, unit circles in a given triangle, and analogous questions for spheres, cones, cylinders, regular pyramids, and more general planar or spatial figures. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's exact nonstandard packing condition is "at most tangential by twos"; to make the question stand-alone, this should be unpacked as a precise pairwise non-overlap condition with tangency allowed. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The paper does not explicitly specify whether n ranges over positive integers or all positive reals; it is only presented as the radius parameter of the containing circle. A fully self-contained restatement should choose and state that domain explicitly. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

In the Bencze variant, i(n) is a radius function depending on n, not an index. A stand-alone formulation should say explicitly that one is given a prescribed function i(n) and still asks for the maximum number of circles of radius i(n) that fit in a circle of radius n. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The paper says the smaller circles are "included into" the larger circle or triangle; a self-contained formulation should spell out full containment of each small circle, with boundary contact allowed. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The triangle variant is specifically "a given triangle" and is flagged parenthetically as being "on Malfatti's problem"; that contextual qualifier is missing from the draft. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))

The paper presents the later items as immediate analogues of the same packing problem, ending with the exact broadening "planar figures included into a given planar figure. And in the space, too." A faithful rewrite should retain that scope and not broaden it further than the paper does. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
refined_question: For a given radius parameter n>0, determine the maximum number M(n) of circles of radius 1 that can be wholly contained in a circle of radius n, under the condition that the small circles are pairwise interior-disjoint and may meet only by tangency (the paper's phrase is "at most tangential by twos"). In the generalized form stated in the paper, determine the analogous maximum when the small circles have radius i(n), where i(n) is a prescribed function of n; then study the same type of packing question for unit circles contained in a given triangle (in connection with Malfatti's problem), and similarly for spheres, cones, cylinders, regular pyramids, and, more generally, for planar figures contained in a given planar figure and for corresponding spatial packings. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
justification: arXiv:math/0010143 is not a paper with a Conjecture 1.1 / Proposition 1.2 / Theorem 1.3 structure; it is organized as a list of numbered "UNSOLVED PROBLEM" items, introduced as a collection of open questions in number theory and geometry. The draft matches Unsolved Problem 8 almost verbatim: the unit-circle-in-circle question appears first, and on the same pages the paper immediately adds the Bencze i(n) version, the triangle version tied to Malfatti's problem, and the extensions to spheres, cones, cylinders, regular pyramids, and general planar/spatial figures. I therefore kept the rewrite anchored to Unsolved Problem 8 specifically, clarified only the paper's nonstandard tangency wording, and did not import any broader packing variants that the paper itself does not state. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/36UnsolvedProblems.pdf))
